text: To decipher something is to work out what it says when it is hard to read — messy handwriting, faded ink, a secret code. It comes from the same root as cipher, meaning a code, so it suggests cracking something rather than just reading it. The worry here is that a kid who never learns cursive will look at a great-grandparent’s letter and see only loops where the words should be.

Something intricate has many small parts fitted closely together, so it takes a while to take in. A spider’s web, a thousand-piece puzzle and a plan with lots of steps are all intricate. Here it describes Tolstoy’s handwriting: his pages were as packed and tangled as the enormous novels he wrote on them.

To shun something is to keep away from it or leave it out on purpose, not by accident. People get shunned too, when a group decides to have nothing to do with them. Saying the Common Core standards shunned cursive means the people writing them chose to drop it and put keyboard skills in its place.

Cursive is handwriting in which the letters are joined together in one flowing line, so the pen barely leaves the paper. Print handwriting is the opposite: each letter stands separately, the way letters look in a book. Almost the whole argument in this article is about whether schools should still teach the joined-up kind.

Confucius was a Chinese thinker who lived about 2,500 years ago, and his sayings about how to behave and how to govern shaped Chinese life for centuries. He is quoted at the top of the article warning people not to trust a man whose writing wobbles. It is a joke about how old the idea is that handwriting reveals character.

Common Core is a set of shared school standards released in America in 2010, listing what students should know in math and English at each grade. Many states agreed to use it so that a sixth-grader in one state would be learning roughly what a sixth-grader in another was. Cursive was not on the list, which is how it dropped out of so many classrooms.

The Declaration of Independence is the 1776 document in which Britain’s thirteen American colonies announced they were breaking away to become their own country. The original is handwritten in elegant cursive and sits on display in Washington, DC. People who want cursive taught often point at it: if you cannot read the script, you cannot read the original.

Colonialism is one country taking control of another place and running it, usually for its own profit, and sending its people, laws and language there. Britain and France each ruled large parts of the world this way for hundreds of years. That is how English handwriting ended up being taught in India and French handwriting in parts of South America.

Écriture ronde is French for round writing, a rounded and decorative style of handwriting developed in France hundreds of years ago. French clerks used it for official documents because it looked neat and impressive. Like English round hand, it travelled wherever France ruled.

The Nazis were the political party, led by Adolf Hitler, that ruled Germany from 1933 to 1945 and started the second world war. They controlled almost everything in daily life, right down to which letters schoolchildren were allowed to form. Their 1941 ban on German cursive is the article’s example of a government reaching into something as small as note-taking.

Latin script is the alphabet you are reading now — A, B, C and the rest — used for English, French, Spanish and many other languages. It is called Latin because it came from the Romans. Older German writing used a different, spikier set of letter shapes, so switching to Latin script made German easier for other Europeans to read.

Critical thinking means not just taking in information but testing it: asking where a claim came from, whether the evidence really supports it, and what someone might have left out. Teachers treat it as a skill to be practised, like free throws. It comes up here because lawmakers claim writing by hand helps students think that way.

Fine motor co-ordination is control of the small, precise movements your fingers and hands make — threading a needle, tying a shoelace, forming a letter. It is the opposite of gross motor skills, which are the big movements of running and throwing. Handwriting is one of the most demanding fine motor tasks a young kid does all day.

Pupils here means students, the school kind. British writers use the word far more than American ones, who usually say students. It has nothing to do with the pupil of your eye, which is a completely separate word that happens to be spelled the same.

A script, in this article, is a style of handwriting or a set of letter shapes — not the pages of dialogue an actor memorises. So gothic script and Latin script are two different ways of drawing the same letters. Watch for the word switching meanings depending on what you are reading.

Engaged here means busy and actively working, the way a machine is engaged when it is switched on and doing its job. It is not the getting-married sense. Saying the brain is engaged in a completely different way means different parts of it were active during handwriting than during typing.

Uniform as a describing word means the same all the way through, with no variation. A row of houses built to one design is uniform; so is snow that falls at the same depth everywhere. The Nazis wanted German writing to be uniform so that anyone across occupied Europe could read it, which has nothing to do with school clothes.

To consume something is to use it up, whether that is food, fuel, money or time. The article uses both senses a few paragraphs apart: Hemingway consumed booze, meaning he drank it, and cursive consumes lesson time, meaning it eats up hours that could go to something else. Same word, two very different things being used up.

To trace something is to follow its path backwards to where it started, step by step. You can trace a river to its source or trace a rumour to the person who began it. Tracing history through handwriting means following letter shapes back through the countries and centuries that passed them along.

Occupied land is land that a foreign army has taken over and is controlling. During the second world war, Germany occupied much of Europe, running countries like France and Poland from the outside. The word is much heavier than occupied meaning busy or in use.

A reed is a tall, thin grass that grows in water at the edge of ponds and rivers. Reeds bend and wave in even a light wind, which is why Confucius picked one for his warning: he distrusted a man whose writing wobbled the same way.

A manuscript is the handwritten or typed version of a book before it is printed — the author’s own copy. The word comes from Latin for written by hand. Tolstoy’s manuscripts were the messy pages he actually wrote War and Peace on.

An epic is a very long story, usually about big events and a great many characters. Ancient poems like the Odyssey are epics, and so are Tolstoy’s enormous novels. Calling his handwriting as dense and intricate as his epics is a joke: both were huge and hard to get through.

Booze is a casual, slightly cheeky word for alcoholic drinks. It is the kind of word you would see in a magazine but not in a science report. Hemingway was famous for drinking a lot, so the article jokes that his handwriting sloped downhill whether or not he had been at it.

Something obsolete is out of date and no longer used, because something better replaced it. Floppy disks and video-rental shops are obsolete. The article says you might assume handwriting questions are obsolete in the age of tablets, then argues that they are not.

Parchment is a writing surface made from thin, scraped, dried animal skin, used across Europe for centuries before cheap paper existed. It was tough and expensive, and important documents were written on it. Saying an age of iPads rather than parchment is a quick way of saying modern rather than ancient.

Penmanship is the skill of writing neatly by hand, judged on how the letters look. Schools once graded it like spelling. The article uses it for the careful lettering of old scribes and of the American constitution.

A scribe was a person whose job was copying documents out by hand, back before printing presses existed. Every copy of a book, law or record had to be written out one at a time, so scribes were highly trained and in demand. Their working habits are the reason cursive exists at all.

A quill is a pen made from a large bird’s feather, cut to a point at the tip and dipped in ink. It holds only a little ink and the point wears down, so lifting it off the page between letters wasted both. Joining the letters made one dip of ink go further.

When something proliferates it spreads and multiplies quickly, turning up in more and more places. Phone apps proliferated once smartphones got cheap. Once metal pen tips and ballpoints arrived, simpler handwriting styles proliferated, because you no longer needed to save ink by joining letters.

Dictation is speaking words out loud for someone, or something, else to write down. Voice-dictation software does it with a microphone: you talk, and the text appears. It is one of the reasons people question whether handwriting still matters.

Calligraphy is handwriting treated as an art form, where the point is beauty rather than speed. It is practised with special pens or brushes and has a long tradition in China, Japan, the Arab world and Europe. The article notes that calligraphy classes are booming in Vietnam.

Something ornate is heavily decorated, covered in curls, patterns or detail. A plain wooden chair is the opposite of an ornate carved one. French schools often teach an ornate cursive, full of loops and flourishes rather than plain strokes.

Something coveted is wanted badly by a lot of people. A coveted spot on the team is one everybody is competing for. Saying cursive is a coveted skill in some countries means people there are eager to have it, not grudgingly made to learn it.

A curriculum is the official list of what students are supposed to learn, and in what order, at each grade. The word comes from a Latin phrase for a running course, like a track you go around. In America there is no single national curriculum — each of the fifty states writes its own.

To mandate something is to officially order that it must be done. A mandate is that order, usually from a government or someone else in charge. States mandating the teaching of cursive are not just suggesting it — schools there have no choice.

A province is a large region a country is divided into, with its own local government. Canada and Argentina have provinces the way the United States has states. Each one can make its own decisions about schools, which is why some brought cursive back while others did not.

To reinstate something is to bring it back after it had been taken away. A player suspended from the team gets reinstated when the ban ends. Provinces that reinstated cursive had dropped it earlier and then changed their minds.

To revamp something is to redo it and give it a fresh shape, keeping the general idea but changing how it works. A revamped website has the same information arranged in a new way. Britain revamped its writing framework, meaning officials rewrote the rules for how handwriting gets taught.

To cite something is to point to it as evidence for what you are claiming. Scientists cite earlier studies; a lawyer cites a law. Oft-cited simply means often cited, so an oft-cited study is one that gets pointed to again and again — which is not the same as one that has been proved.

A neuroscientist is a scientist who studies the brain and the nervous system — how signals travel through it and how it produces memory, movement and learning. Neuro comes from the Greek word for nerve. Audrey van der Meer is the one whose brain-scan study lawmakers keep quoting.

To be sceptical is to doubt a claim and want better evidence before accepting it. It is not the same as saying the claim is wrong — it means not convinced yet. Spelled skeptical in America and sceptical in Britain, which is why it looks odd here.

Cognitive means having to do with thinking: remembering, reasoning, paying attention, solving problems. So cognitively more capable means better at thinking, not stronger or faster. Professor Graham doubts that the particular shape of your letters could change that.

To fret is to worry about something, usually on and on rather than all at once. Parents fret about grades; you might fret about a game all week. Here people fret that kids who never learn cursive will not be able to read their own family history.

To meddle is to interfere in something that is not really your business. A neighbour who rearranges your garden is meddling. Saying the Nazis meddled with note-taking makes their handwriting ban sound like a government poking into something it had no business touching.

Legible writing is clear enough to be read. Its opposite is illegible, which is what a doctor’s scrawl is usually accused of being. The Nazis wanted a script that was legible to people all over occupied Europe, not just to Germans.

To write something off is to decide it is finished or worthless and stop counting on it. People write off an old car, or write off a team after a bad start. The article is making a pun: handwriting is not being written off, meaning it is not being dismissed after all.

To choose one thing in favour of another is to pick the second one instead. You might skip a movie in favour of a nap. Common Core dropped cursive in favour of keyboard skills, meaning keyboards took the time cursive used to get. Favour is the British spelling of favor.

If something is at your disposal, it is available for you to use whenever you like. A team with three good goalkeepers at its disposal can pick any of them. It has nothing to do with throwing things away, even though disposal usually does.

Something in vogue is fashionable right now. The phrase is borrowed from French and shows up in writing about clothes, music and ideas. Asking why cursive is back in vogue is asking why it suddenly became popular again.

To resort to something is to fall back on it because the better option did not work out. You resort to walking when the bus never comes. Adults who resort to squat, boxy scripts are not choosing that handwriting so much as ending up with it.

The last line plays on the set phrase the right stuff, which means having exactly the qualities a hard job demands. Swapping right for write turns it into a joke about handwriting lessons. Puns like this are common in Economist headlines and closing lines.
